title: A Rank-k Correction Deserves a Rank-k Inverse

body:
A $d \times d$ matrix $A$ sits in memory with its inverse — or at least a Cholesky factor — already paid for. Someone hands you a rank-$k$ correction $UCV^\top$, with $k \ll d$, and asks for the inverse of $A + UCV^\top$. The naive move, re-inverting at $O(d^3)$, is almost always wrong. The right move is a formula a century old, due in various forms to Duncan, Guttman, Woodbury, Sherman, and Morrison, and it is the quiet linear-algebra engine behind exact Gaussian process regression, every Kalman filter in production, recursive least squares, portfolio updates, and several of the tricks that make LoRA adapters composable.

The identity does one thing: it trades a $d \times d$ inverse for a $k \times k$ inverse. The payoff is the gap between $d$ and $k$. Where that gap is wide — a Kalman filter with few new measurements per step, a GP that grows one point at a time, a LoRA adapter with $r \in \{4, 8, 16\}$ on top of a $d \in \{4096, 8192\}$ weight matrix — the identity is the difference between a method that scales and a method that does not.

## Why the asymmetry matters

Modern ML has quietly concentrated computation on exactly the problem Woodbury is written for. LoRA adapters are rank-$r$ with $r \ll d$. GP conditioning adds a handful of rows at a time to a growing covariance. Kalman filters update by $m$ measurements with $m \ll n$. In each setting the big matrix is fixed and known; the small correction is new. Recomputing the full inverse ignores that structure. The identity extracts it.

Numerical practice compounds the point. Keeping $A^{-1}$ — or a factorisation — around and applying rank-$k$ patches is cheaper, more stable, and in the Kalman setting it is the entire reason the information form of the filter exists.

## The identity

Let $A \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times d}$, $U \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$, $V \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times k}$, $C \in \mathbb{R}^{k \times k}$. Assuming $A$, $C$, and the capacitance matrix $C^{-1} + V^\top A^{-1} U$ are all invertible,

$$
(A + UCV^\top)^{-1} \;=\; A^{-1} - A^{-1} U \,\bigl(C^{-1} + V^\top A^{-1} U\bigr)^{-1} V^\top A^{-1}.
$$

The rank-one special case, due to Sherman and Morrison in 1950, is the version most people meet first:

$$
(A + uv^\top)^{-1} \;=\; A^{-1} - \frac{A^{-1} u \, v^\top A^{-1}}{1 + v^\top A^{-1} u}.
$$

Proof by direct verification: multiply $(A + UCV^\top)$ by the claimed inverse on the right. The cross-terms cancel exactly. A more revealing derivation inverts the block matrix

$$
\begin{pmatrix} A & U \\ -V^\top & C^{-1} \end{pmatrix}
$$

in two different ways — first eliminating $A$, then eliminating $C^{-1}$ — and equates the top-left entries of the resulting block inverses. The second route makes the role of the capacitance matrix (the Schur complement of $A$ in that block system) explicit, and that is the matrix that governs the identity's numerical behaviour.

Cost: forming the inverse via Woodbury runs in $O(d^2 k + k^3)$ versus $O(d^3)$. For $k \ll d$ the saving is the whole point. If what you need is not the inverse but a solve, replace each explicit inverse with a factorisation and the same algebra carries through.

## Three places it earns its keep

**Kalman filter, information form.** The covariance-form measurement update is

$$
P_{k|k} \;=\; P_{k|k-1} - P_{k|k-1} H^\top (H P_{k|k-1} H^\top + R)^{-1} H P_{k|k-1}.
$$

Applying Woodbury with $A = P_{k|k-1}^{-1}$, $U = V = H^\top$, $C = R^{-1}$ gives the information-form update

$$
P_{k|k}^{-1} \;=\; P_{k|k-1}^{-1} + H^\top R^{-1} H,
$$

which is additive in the information matrix $\Lambda = P^{-1}$. The subtraction in the covariance form is a classical source of loss-of-positive-definiteness under roundoff; the additive information form sidesteps it. Numerical analysts have been arguing since the 1970s about which form is more stable, but the practical point is that both forms are *the same identity*, read in opposite directions.

**Gaussian process regression, online.** Conditioning a GP on $n$ data points requires the inverse of an $n \times n$ Gram matrix $K$. When one new point arrives, the enlarged matrix differs from $\begin{pmatrix} K & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}$ by a rank-two correction — one row and one column, which decomposes as $UV^\top$ with $U, V \in \mathbb{R}^{(n+1) \times 2}$. Updating $K^{-1}$ via Woodbury costs $O(n^2)$ per new point rather than the $O(n^3)$ of a full re-inversion, and that is how most online GP implementations hold up for $n$ into the tens of thousands before structured kernels or inducing points have to take over.

**LoRA and natural-gradient preconditioners.** A LoRA-adapted linear layer is $W' = W + BA$ with $B \in \mathbb{R}^{d \times r}$, $A \in \mathbb{R}^{r \times d}$, and $r \in \{4, 8, 16, 32\}$. In most forward and backward passes you never form $(W')^{-1}$ — the gain of LoRA is that you *don't* materialise $BA$. But $(W')^{-1}$ appears in natural-gradient and Fisher preconditioners, in closed-form adapter-merge routines, in some unlearning procedures, and in iterative refinement of attention logits, and Woodbury gives it directly:

$$
(W + BA)^{-1} \;=\; W^{-1} - W^{-1} B \,(I_r + A W^{-1} B)^{-1} A W^{-1}.
$$

The capacitance matrix is $r \times r$. For $r = 8$ and $d = 4096$, that is an $8 \times 8$ inverse instead of a $4096 \times 4096$ one — a ratio of $(d/r)^3 \approx 1.3 \times 10^8$ in theoretical cost. The same identity sits at the core of K-FAC and other block-diagonal natural-gradient methods: whenever you keep a factored estimate of a Fisher block and add a rank-one gradient outer product, the update to its inverse is Sherman–Morrison.

## A concrete anchor

A small sanity check in NumPy:

```python
import numpy as np

d, k = 2000, 8
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
A = rng.standard_normal((d, d))
A = A @ A.T + d * np.eye(d)      # SPD, well-conditioned
U = rng.standard_normal((d, k))
V = rng.standard_normal((d, k))
C = np.eye(k)

# Direct inverse (expensive).
M = A + U @ C @ V.T
inv_direct = np.linalg.inv(M)

# Woodbury update.
A_inv = np.linalg.inv(A)
cap = np.linalg.inv(C) + V.T @ A_inv @ U        # k x k capacitance
inv_wb = A_inv - A_inv @ U @ np.linalg.solve(cap, V.T @ A_inv)

print(np.max(np.abs(inv_direct - inv_wb)))      # ~1e-11
```

On a laptop the direct inverse costs seconds; the Woodbury update costs tens of milliseconds. The error is roundoff, as expected.

The anchor also shows the hazard. If you scale $C$ so that $C^{-1} + V^\top A^{-1} U$ approaches singularity — algebraically possible whenever $A + UCV^\top$ is well-conditioned but the capacitance matrix is not — the small $k \times k$ inverse becomes the dominant source of error. The identity is exact; its arithmetic is only as good as the capacitance matrix's condition number.

## What to reach for

If you expect rank-$k$ patches to a matrix whose inverse (or factorisation) you already have, keep the inverse, not the matrix, and apply Woodbury. For symmetric positive-definite problems — Kalman filtering, GPs, Fisher-information preconditioners — prefer the information form or a square-root factor update, which do the same algebra in a numerically kinder basis. Monitor the capacitance matrix: a quick check of its condition number tells you whether you still trust the update. And remember that the identity does not extend to Moore–Penrose pseudoinverses of rank-deficient matrices without extra care; specialised formulas are needed when the update changes rank.

A diagnostic worth running when a method mysteriously loses accuracy after many updates: compute $\|M - (A + UCV^\top)\|$ for the current $M$ and compare to $\|A\|$ and $\|UCV^\top\|$ separately. If the error has grown faster than $\kappa(\text{cap}) \cdot \varepsilon_{\text{machine}}$, Woodbury is not where your bug is. If it tracks that bound, it probably is, and you want iterative refinement or a periodic re-factorisation of the full matrix to clear drift. In production Kalman filters this periodic "reset" is standard — the information filter is run in square-root form between resets precisely because the long chain of Woodbury-equivalent updates slowly loses digits even when each individual step is well-conditioned.

## Limits and open questions

Numerical stability is the open front. A recent note titled *A Note on the Stability of the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury Formula* (arXiv:2504.04554, 2025) extends classical analyses of Yip and Hager to full-rank updates and sharpens the bound: the forward error of Woodbury is governed by the condition number of the capacitance matrix, not of $A + UCV^\top$ itself. When those two differ sharply, naive Woodbury loses digits; iterative refinement or a mixed-precision correction recovers them. The precise sharp constant for the general case remains open.

The pseudoinverse case is also unfinished. Woodbury fails for Moore–Penrose pseudoinverses when the correction changes rank; Güttel and collaborators (arXiv:2406.15120, 2024) propose a tailored update rule for the full-rank-rectangular case and argue it reduces the cost of least squares with low-rank updates from $O(mn^2)$ to $O(mnr)$, with empirically small forward error. A general stability analysis for rank-changing updates is still open.

Finally, scale eventually bites. The identity converts an $O(d^3)$ problem into $O(d^2 k + k^3)$, but when $d^2$ is already punishing — the full Gram matrix of a million-point GP — even Woodbury is too expensive, and inducing-point methods, Krylov solvers, and conjugate-gradient preconditioners take over. The identity remains correct; it stops being the right identity.

There is a methodological reading too. The choice between covariance form and information form in a Kalman filter is Woodbury read left-to-right or right-to-left, and the "better" direction depends on which matrix is easier to keep well-conditioned under the problem's noise. The same translates to LoRA inversion: whether to maintain $W^{-1}$ and patch, or to maintain a factor of $W'$ and refactor, is a problem-specific trade. Woodbury only tells you the two bookkeepings are equivalent; it does not tell you which one your data prefers.

## Further reading

- *A Note on the Stability of the Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury Formula*, 2025. arXiv:2504.04554. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.04554>. The modern error analysis — the capacitance matrix is where the roundoff lives — and the right paper to read before trusting Woodbury on an ill-conditioned problem.
- Güttel et al., *A Sherman–Morrison–Woodbury approach to solving least squares problems with low-rank updates*, 2024. arXiv:2406.15120, accepted at IMA JNA; code at github.com/nla-group/WoodburyLS. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.15120>. The pseudoinverse case that classical Woodbury does not cover, with a cost analysis.
- *Kalman filter demystified: from intuition to probabilistic graphical model to real case in financial markets*. arXiv:1811.11618. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1811.11618>. A readable walk through covariance- and information-form filters, with the stability argument spelled out.
- *Constructing numerically stable Kalman filter-based algorithms for gradient-based adaptive filtering.* arXiv:1303.4622. <https://arxiv.org/abs/1303.4622>. Where the covariance form breaks under roundoff, and what to do.
- D'Souza and Zanetti, *A UDU-factorized information filter*, NEAR technical report, University of Texas, 2018. <https://sites.utexas.edu/near/files/2018/05/UDU_Information.pdf>. The square-root information filter in practice; standard in orbit determination for stability reasons.
- *Linear Time GPs for Inferring Latent Trajectories from Neural Spike Trains.* arXiv:2306.01802. <https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.01802>. The Woodbury-derived low-cost recursion for GP inference, as applied in neuroscience.
